Can memistor-class electrochemical weights train neural networks?

Questeria and Claude (Anthropic)

October 2026

Abstract

In 1960 Widrow and Hoff stored the weights of their adaptive neuron in memistors, three-terminal electrochemical cells; their modern descendants are lithium-ion, metal-oxide and protonic ECRAM. We ask, in simulation, how close such devices come to digital training when every weight update is made of device pulses, while the forward and backward reads are kept ideal (fp32). We compare plain SGD and three Tiki-Taka-family algorithms on five device specifications (two AIHWKIT fits mapped one to one, one measured array, a protonic-inspired scenario and an optimistic historical scenario), on MNIST, a CIFAR-10 subset and a byte-level language model, with five seeds that share initialisation and data order across arms. Against SGD with exact updates at the same learning rate, pairings (Li-ECRAM and protonic-inspired, each with chopped TTv2 or AGAD) stay within the pre-set margins on all three tasks, and plain SGD exceeds them on every published device. Against a separately tuned digital Adam no pairing does: on the language model the best analog result is  % worse in bits per byte. After per-arm tuning we detect no growth of the gap with width over a factor of four, without establishing equivalence. A sensitivity sheet against absolute accuracy lines, with three seeds, establishes only a few one-at-a-time ranges (on CIFAR with chopped TTv2, step asymmetry up to and reference error up to ), and shows that an earlier asymmetry limit was mostly lost weight range. A conditional energy projection for the weight-matrix operations, borrowing the read efficiency of an analog inference chip, gives about –\(\times\) less energy per weight-row than an H100, reported only where the quality is reached. This version repairs the simulator after an independent review (matched random streams, a physically applied reset, the device presets mapped one to one) and reports how much each repair moved the original results. We propose, but did not build, a bench replication protocol of the 1960 memistor.

Introduction

Training a neural network on a digital processor moves every weight from memory to arithmetic and back at every update. In 1960, Widrow and Hoff took a different route: they stored each weight of their adaptive ADALINE neuron in a memistor, an electrochemical cell whose conductance is set by the time integral of a current through a third terminal [1], [2], [3]. The weight was read without being disturbed, and it was adapted in place. The device was macroscopic, the cells were wet, and no multilayer learning rule existed yet, so the line ended with the Madaline hardware of the early 1960s [3]. That machine was a working analog learning system.

Sixty years later, three-terminal electrochemical devices have returned at the nanoscale. Lithium-ion ECRAM [4], [5], CMOS-compatible metal-oxide ECRAM [6], protonic programmable resistors [7], [8] and open-loop programmable arrays [9] all decouple the read path from the write path, just as the memistor did. They report hundreds to thousands of conductance levels, nanosecond pulses and femtojoule-scale write energies. In parallel, algorithms for training on imperfect analog weights have matured: the stochastic pulse-coincidence update of the resistive processing unit (RPU) [10], Tiki-Taka [11] and its successors TTv2 [12], chopped TTv2 and AGAD [13], and residual learning with convergence guarantees [14].

That electrochemical weights can train small networks is already established: Chen et al. trained in situ on an ECRAM array and simulated larger networks [9], and Rasch et al. studied reference correction, retention and device requirements for the TT family [13]. Most recently, Wu et al. [15] simulated ECRAM-calibrated Transformers of up to about 123 million parameters with finite converters and device nonidealities, keeping the weight-gradient path digital. Our contribution is narrower and specific: a reproducible, seed-matched simulation comparison of plain SGD and three device-tolerant algorithms on a catalog of published (or, where nothing is published, labelled hypothetical) electrochemical devices, with the weight update done entirely in the devices, on three small tasks; a sensitivity analysis against absolute accuracy lines; and a conditional energy projection. Results are stated against two digital baselines: SGD with exact updates at the same learning rate, and a separately tuned Adam.

What this paper provides:

  1. A simulator with stated limits. Reads are ideal (fp32); only the update is analog. It reproduces selected published outcomes of Gokmen and Haensch 2020 under this simplified read model, and the offset-robustness ordering of Rasch et al. 2024 (Section 4.1). After an independent review it was repaired (separate random streams, a reset made of pulses, the AIHWKIT device presets mapped one to one) and each repair is tested (Section 3, Appendix 7).

  2. A seed-matched comparison of SGD, TTv2, chopped TTv2 and AGAD on five device specifications, three tasks (MNIST, a CIFAR-10 subset, a byte-level language model on human-written text) and five seeds, with every arm of a seed sharing its initial weights and data order (Section 4.2).

  3. A width study with per-arm learning rates and an equivalence test (Section 4.3).

  4. A sensitivity sheet against absolute accuracy lines, with the asymmetry sweep repeated at a fixed symmetry point so that asymmetry is not confounded with lost weight range (Section 4.4).

  5. A conditional energy projection for the weight-matrix operations, reported only where the device reaches the stated quality (Section [sec:energy]).

  6. A proposed roadmap of device experiments and a proposed, unbuilt bench replication protocol of the 1960 memistor (Section [sec:roadmap], Appendix [app:bench]).

Every experiment was planned in a committed plan before it ran; the plans are internal, timestamped by the repository, not an external registry. The original runs and the revision runs are kept apart, and every deviation is recorded (Section [sec:availability]). All results are simulations, and every device parameter carries a provenance label (measured, fitted, claimed, estimated or assumed).

Background and related work

The memistor (1960)

Widrow and Hoff introduced the ADALINE and the least-mean-squares (LMS) rule in 1960 [2]. To store its weights they built the memistor [1]. A pencil-lead (graphite) substrate sits in a copper-sulphate plating bath. Copper is plated onto it or removed from it by a current through a third electrode, and the conductance between the lead’s two ends is sensed with a small AC signal that does not disturb the state. Widrow, Pierce and Angell described elements with “thousands” of analog levels that spanned roughly 100 to 1 ohm in about ten seconds at a few milliamperes; this description is reported in secondary sources, see [16]. Mouttet analyses the memistor as a three-terminal memristive system and summarises Widrow’s ideal: a conductance linear in the plating charge, reversible, non-volatile and free of hysteresis [16]. Widrow and Lehr recount that the Madaline I machine was built in hardware with memistor weights and used for pattern recognition research [3]. Write noise, up/down asymmetry, retention and endurance were never reported in a form we could find, so in our catalog these are estimates (Section 3.4). The memistor predates Chua’s memristor [17] and its later physical identification in titanium-oxide films [18]. It is the conceptual ancestor of today’s three-terminal synaptic transistors.

Device requirements for training

Gokmen and Vlasov [10] defined the resistive processing unit (RPU). Updates are stochastic pulse trains whose coincidences change the conductance by a fixed step (stochastic computing, [19]). They derived device specifications for plain SGD on MNIST at a small error penalty: about a thousand levels, up/down asymmetry of a few percent, and tolerance to large cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variation. Agarwal et al. [20] reached similar conclusions; the requirements were extended to convolutional networks [21], and reviews cover the device landscape [22], [23], [24], [25]. Mixed-precision schemes [26] accumulate the gradient digitally and program the devices rarely. They relax the device demands but give up the fully parallel in-memory update.

Algorithms that tolerate asymmetric devices

Real devices change their conductance by different amounts up and down, and the step depends on the state (soft bounds). Under plain SGD this acts as an implicit penalty that pulls weights toward each device’s symmetry point [11], [14].

  • Tiki-Taka (TTv1) [11] uses two arrays. The gradient is accumulated on an array \(A\), and its columns are periodically transferred into the weight array \(C\), with \(W=\gamma A+C\). Asymmetry then acts as a useful decay on \(A\) instead of a bias on \(W\).

  • TTv2 [12] inserts a digital buffer \(H\) between the two arrays. \(H\) low-pass filters the reads of \(A\), and a pulse is sent to \(C\) only when a threshold is crossed. TTv2 still needs every device’s symmetry point to be subtracted by a reference.

  • Chopped TTv2 (c-TTv2) and AGAD [13], [27] remove this sensitivity. A random sign modulates the inputs and the reads (c-TTv2). AGAD additionally replaces the static reference with a digital, on-the-fly reference taken from the recent history of \(A\).

  • Residual learning [14] gives convergence guarantees for this family.

IBM’s open-source AIHWKIT [28] implements these algorithms with fitted device presets, including the Li-ECRAM and metal-oxide ECRAM presets whose parameters we use. In the revision these two presets are mapped one to one onto AIHWKIT’s own LinearStepDevice model, with its shifted bounds and slope spread, and checked against AIHWKIT’s pulse responses (Section 3.4).

Electrochemical three-terminal devices

  • Lithium-ion synaptic transistors and ECRAM. Fuller et al. [5] showed a lithium-ion synaptic transistor, followed by an ionic floating-gate array [29]. Tang et al. [4] reported Li-WO\(_3\) ECRAM with about a thousand symmetric, linear states and nanosecond pulses.

  • Metal-oxide ECRAM. Kim et al. [6] made it CMOS-compatible.

  • Protonic resistors. Onen et al. [7] reported nanosecond protonic programmable resistors with a phosphosilicate-glass electrolyte. In 2026, Xu et al. [8] quantified cycle-to-cycle (3%) and device-to-device (21%) variability of BEOL-compatible protonic ECRAM.

  • Open-loop programmable arrays. Chen et al. [9] demonstrated a \(10\times10\) W/YSZ/WO\(_x\) array with 256 states.

  • Organic devices. Organic electrochemical synapses [30] extend the family to low voltages.

In-situ training on ECRAM hardware has so far been shown on small arrays, for example a \(3\times3\) array by Li et al. [31] and the \(10\times10\) array of [9]. Other memory technologies have gone further. Phase-change and resistive arrays have trained or run networks at larger scale [32], [33], [34], [35], and analog-AI inference chips with on-chip periphery now report measured efficiencies of about 10 TOPS/W [36], [37].

Scaling analog training.

Wu et al. [15] co-designed the weight mapping, the optimizer and the converters, and simulated ECRAM-calibrated Transformers up to about 123 million parameters with finite converter resolution and device nonidealities. Their weight-gradient path stays digital, so they do not test the fully in-memory update studied here. The two studies answer complementary questions: what an analog update saves in computation and data movement, and what it costs in accuracy and calibration. Our models are far smaller (Section [sec:discussion]).

Methods

Device model

Each analog weight is one device with a normalised state \(u\in[-1,1]\) between its own bounds. Its conductance is \(g=g_{\min}+\tfrac{u+1}{2}(g_{\max}-g_{\min})\), and the weight is read differentially as \(w=\alpha\,(g-g_{\mathrm{ref}})\). One nominal pulse moves \(u\) by \(k=2/n_{\mathrm{states}}\) at mid-range. With asymmetry \(a\) the up and down steps are \(k_\pm=k\,s\,(1\pm a/2)\), where \(s\) is a per-device step factor with spread \(\sigma_{\mathrm{d2d}}\). With saturation (soft bounds) the steps depend on the state: \[\Delta u_+ = k_+\,(1-\gamma_+ u),\qquad \Delta u_- = -k_-\,(1+\gamma_- u).\] The per-device slopes \(\gamma_\pm\) have a relative spread \(\sigma_\gamma\). A device’s symmetry point, where an up and a down pulse cancel, is \(u^*=(k_+-k_-)/(k_+\gamma_++k_-\gamma_-)\). The reference \(g_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is set at \(g(u^*)\) plus a calibration error of standard deviation \(\sigma_r\), in units of the half-range. A constant-step device has no symmetry point and is referenced at mid-range.

  • Several pulses in one update. When a device receives \(n_+\) up and \(n_-\) down pulses in one update, the pulses are taken as uniformly interleaved, and \(\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}s=A-Bu\) is solved exactly over the batch, with \(A=k_+n_+-k_-n_-\) and \(B=k_+\gamma_+n_++k_-\gamma_-n_-\).

  • Write noise. Cycle-to-cycle noise adds a Gaussian with standard deviation \(c_{2c}\) times the local step, growing as the square root of the pulse count.

  • Drift. Retention loss relaxes \(u\) toward the bare state \(u=-1\) with a time constant \(\tau\) in training steps.

  • Bounds. The bounds \(g_{\min}\), \(g_{\max}\) carry a device-to-device spread.

The AIHWKIT LinearStepDevice (revision).

The two devices taken from AIHWKIT presets (Li-ECRAM, MO-ECRAM) use AIHWKIT’s own parameterisation instead: the state is the weight itself, with hard bounds \(b_{\max}=w_{\max}(1+\sigma_b\xi)\) and \(b_{\min}=w_{\min}(1+\sigma_b\xi)\) around shifted means (\(w_{\max}=\RVliWmax\), \(w_{\min}=\RVliWmin\) for Li-ECRAM, so that the symmetry point is at zero), steps \(k(1\pm\beta+\sigma_{\mathrm{d2d}}\xi)\), and slopes divided by the mean bounds, \(\Delta w_+=k_+(1-|\gamma_++\sigma_{\gamma+}\xi|\,w/w_{\max})\) and \(\Delta w_-=-k_-(1+|\gamma_-+\sigma_{\gamma-}\xi|\,w/|w_{\min}|)\), with multiplicative write noise. The original version of this paper copied the preset fields into the model above with bounds \([-1,1]\) and no slope spread; that mapping is kept only for comparison (Appendix 7).

Forward and backward passes read the weights ideally, in fp32. Read noise and DAC/ADC quantisation are outside the scope of this study, which isolates the update; the energy projection (Section [sec:energy]) nevertheless prices finite-precision reads, so accuracy and energy rest on different read assumptions. Biases, layer norms and the language model’s position table are digital.

The update

We use the stochastic pulse-coincidence scheme of [10]. Each sample (row) offers \(BL=31\) pulse slots. Input \(i\) fires with probability \(p_{x,i}\propto|x_i|\) and error \(j\) with probability \(p_{d,j}\propto|d_j|\), with the scaling split equally between the two streams (update management). Weight \(ij\) therefore receives coincidences with mean \(\eta\,|x_i d_j|/(\alpha k)\). Up and down counts are kept separate, so asymmetry is never cancelled digitally. Within a batch the counts of all samples are summed and drawn from a Poisson distribution with the requested mean. A mini-batch therefore only groups pulses; it does not average gradients.

This is a surrogate, not a pulse-by-pulse simulation. The mean is exact only while the largest pre-clamp slot probability is at most one, i.e. \((\eta/\alpha k)\max|x|\max|d|\le BL\); beyond that the probabilities are clipped and part of the update is lost. The repaired simulator records, per layer, the fraction of updates that clipped and the lost fraction of the requested update (Section 4.2). Discrete pulses do not commute on a state-dependent device (on a 20-level soft-bounds device one up then one down pulse from \(u=0.4\) ends at RVorderUpDn, the reverse order at RVorderDnUp, and the batch solution at RVorderBatch), and independent per-cell Poisson draws ignore the correlations of shared row and column pulse streams. A larger variance than the binomial one is therefore not claimed to be conservative.

Algorithms

SGD.

The pulses go directly into the weight devices.

TTv1 [11].

The pulses go into an array \(A\), and the forward weight is \(C+\gamma A\). Every batch, \(n_c\) columns \(j\) of \(A\) are read and added to \(C\) by a pulsed outer product, \(\lambda A_{:,j}\,e_j^{\top}\). \(A\) is never reset.

TTv2 (local variant of [12]).

Each read column is added to a digital buffer, \(H_{:,j}\mathrel{+}=\lambda A_{:,j}/(\alpha k)\). \(C\) receives up to 31 pulses where \(|H|\ge1\), and \(H\) keeps the remainder. Optionally the read column of \(A\) is reset after the read. Published TTv2 uses single-pulse transfers, forgets a buffer element after it fires and does not reset \(A\); we name ours a variant and run the published-style form beside it in the diagnostic (Appendix 7).

The reset of \(A\) (revision).

The original simulator moved the read column of \(A\) straight to its symmetry point and charged \(2BL=62\) pulses it never applied (the ideal reset). Applied through the device model, those 62 alternating pulses leave  % of the displacement on the protonic-inspired device. The repaired pulse reset uses the transfer’s own read: a sign-directed train of \(\mathrm{round}(|A_{ij}|/\alpha k)\) pulses toward the read zero, re-read and corrected once, at most 62 pulses per weight, every pulse applied through the device dynamics (with its write noise, state-dependent step and device spread) and counted. The ideal reset is reported only as a labelled variant.

c-TTv2 [13].

Chopper signs \(c_j\in\{\pm1\}\) modulate the inputs of the \(A\) update (\(c\odot x\)) and demodulate the reads (\(c_jA_{:,j}\)). Each read column’s chopper flips with probability \(\rho\).

AGAD [13].

The choppers of c-TTv2, plus a digital leaky average of the reads, \(p_j\leftarrow(1-\beta)p_j+\beta A_{:,j}\). The read is \(z_j=c_j(A_{:,j}-p^{\mathrm{ref}}_j)\), and \(p^{\mathrm{ref}}_j\) is reset to \(p_j\) whenever \(c_j\) flips.

In the main experiments every TT-family \(A\) array uses a learning rate \(1/\lambda\) times larger, so that \(\lambda\times\) (the \(A\) rate) equals the SGD rate; the TTv1 configuration of the published benchmark (Section 4.1) is the exception (\(\eta=0.01\), \(\lambda=0.02\), \(A\) rate equal to \(\eta\)). The settings, including the choice between the pulse reset and no reset, were chosen once on MNIST validation with a mid-quality device that is not in the catalog (Section 3.6; Appendix [app:selection]). We implemented the algorithms from the papers’ text; we did not use the authors’ code.

Device catalog and provenance

Table 1 lists the devices. Every field carries a provenance label:

  • MEASURED: reported in the paper;

  • FIT: from the AIHWKIT presets fitted to the published devices [28];

  • CLAIM: a qualitative statement in the paper, translated by us;

  • ESTIMATE: ours;

  • ASSUMED: for example, the 2% reference error given to every device.

The protonic device of [7] is mostly estimated: the paper reports a thousand up and a thousand down pulses that are “nearly linear and symmetric”, but no write-noise or variability statistics, and its finite retention is replaced by no drift. We therefore call it a protonic-inspired scenario; a thousand applied pulses are not a demonstration of a thousand independently programmable states. In Table 1 the Li-ECRAM and MO-ECRAM rows show the original field copy; the revised runs use the one-to-one AIHWKIT mapping above (bounds \([\RVliWmin, \RVliWmax]\) and \([\RVmoWmin, \RVmoWmax]\), absolute slope spread ). Widrow’s memistor is given two specifications, one as he described it and one pessimistic, together with a pencil-lead cell built today with modern hobby materials (Appendix [app:bench]).

Tasks and baselines

MNIST [38].

A 784–256–128–10 tanh MLP; 10 epochs, batch 128, on 55,000 training images. 5,000 held-out training images form the validation set, and the 10,000 test images are the test set.

CIFAR-10 subset [39].

Three \(3\times3\) convolutions with \(c\), \(2c\) and \(2c\) channels (base \(c=32\)), computed as crossbar matrix products over unfolded patches, then two fully connected layers. 30 epochs, batch 128, on the first 10,000 images of training batches 1–2. The next 2,000 images are the validation set, and the 10,000-image test set is the test set.

Character LM.

A byte-level, two-layer transformer [40] of width \(d\) (base 128) and context 128, trained on 8 MB of enwik8 [41], which is human-written Wikipedia text of 2006. 3,000 steps of \(32\times128\) bytes. Every learned weight matrix uses the device model, including the embedding and the head; the activation-dependent attention products and the other operations are digital. Validation is the slice’s last 0.5 MB, held out from training in selection runs. Test is a separate 0.5 MB slice.

The first baseline (“FP-SGD”) is the same network, initialisation, data order and update rule with an exact floating-point weight update. The second is Adam [42] on digital twins with the same initialisation and data order and its own learning rate selected on validation; in the revision it is reported for all three tasks, beside FP-SGD. The gap is FP accuracy minus device accuracy for classification, in percentage points. For the LM it is the device’s bits per byte relative to FP’s, minus one, in percent.

Protocol and statistics

Every experiment was pre-registered in a committed plan before it ran (Section [sec:availability]).

  • Hyperparameters were chosen on validation splits only, with an edge rule: whenever the best value of a grid lies at its edge, the next half-decade point is added. The learning rate of every device arm in the main table is the FP validation choice. The scale study instead tunes each arm separately.

  • Statistics. The main table uses five seeds per arm. Gaps are paired by seed, and we report the mean and a 95% Student-\(t\) interval. A cell PASSES when the whole interval lies below the gap line (2 pp for classification, 5% for the LM), FAILS when it lies wholly above, and is UNRESOLVED otherwise.

  • Multiplicity. We make no correction for multiplicity. The intervals describe each cell, not the family, and a best cell chosen among many is optimistic.

  • Random streams (revision). Each seed defines separate generators for the logical initialisation, the data order, each tile’s device population and the pulse and noise draws, so the paired gap compares runs that share their initial weights and their data.

  • Width (revision). The endpoint contrast \(D\) (gap at the widest minus the narrowest width) is tested for equivalence (TOST at 5 %, margins equal to the gap lines); “no evidence of growth beyond the margin” when only the upper bound is under the margin; never “flat”.

  • Sensitivity (revision). Each grid point is labelled against the absolute line with 3 seeds paired with FP-SGD of the same seed; a threshold is the weakest value that passes with every value toward the best end passing.

Simulator checks

The simulator is checked by 14 checks, and each check is shown to fail on at least one deliberately planted fault (17 faults in all). Examples of what the checks cover:

  • the exact-update arm equals PyTorch SGD;

  • the mean pulse update equals the SGD step;

  • alternating pulses converge to the analytic symmetry point, including with per-device slopes;

  • write noise grows as \(\sqrt n\);

  • drift relaxes to the bare state;

  • a static read offset is integrated by TTv2, mostly cancelled by c-TTv2 and nearly fully cancelled by AGAD;

  • TTv1 moves \(C\) along \(+\lambda A\);

  • the SGD and TTv2 paths are bit-identical to the earlier code that produced our preliminary results.

The planted faults include a swapped pulse sign, a dropped chopper demodulation and a never-updated AGAD reference. Both suites run at the start of every compute session and stop it on any failure (Appendix [app:checks]). The revision adds checks of the repairs (matched initialisation and data order across arms, a shared device population across algorithms, resets that charge exactly the pulses they apply, the AIHWKIT LinearStepDevice recurrence, the clipping statistics, the published-style buffer, the re-centred symmetry point, and a bit-exact replay of the original simulator), each shown to fail on the old behaviour or a planted fault (Appendix 7). These checks test the implementation; they do not validate the physical model.

Results

Simulator validation

Gokmen and Haensch 2020.

We map their RPU-baseline device onto our model:

  • step \(10^{-3}\) at \(w=0\);

  • mean saturation slope \(1.66\) with a 25% per-device spread;

  • 30% step spread and 30% cycle-to-cycle noise;

  • a symmetry point at \(w=0\) for every device.

We train their 784–256–128–10 sigmoid network on MNIST for 50 epochs at their learning rate of 0.01. The results are in Table 2 and Fig. 1a.

  • FP reaches 1.78% test error, against their 2.0%.

  • SGD on the device reaches 14.47% [12.68, 16.26], against “about 15%”.

  • Tiki-Taka reaches 2.26% [2.13, 2.39], against “close to 2%”.

By our pre-registered criteria the agreement is quantitative: this is agreement with selected published outcomes under a simplified read model, not a full quantitative validation. Matching an endpoint under different sources of error cannot rule out compensating differences, and the batch-64 result below shows how sensitive the SGD arm is to the protocol. These validation runs used the original simulator (TTv1 has no reset, so the reset repair does not touch them). The known differences are listed in Section [sec:limits]:

  • we use mini-batches of 16, not 1;

  • we do not model read noise, ADC/DAC quantisation or analog biases.

At batch 64 the FP and TTv1 results barely move, but SGD on the device degrades further. Summing more samples’ pulses before the weight changes hurts a strongly asymmetric device, which is another reason to use batch 16 as the closer match to their batch 1.

Rasch et al. 2024, qualitatively.

We use a 20-state soft-bounds device with an uncorrected reference offset of \(\sigma_r=0.5\) (Table 3, Fig. 1b).

  • TTv2’s test error rises from 4.12% to 24.27%.

  • c-TTv2 rises less, from 4.29% to 13.02%.

  • AGAD is unaffected: 8.47% versus 7.88%.

This is the published ordering; our pre-registered check reads reproduced. It rests on two seeds per condition and an ordering, so it does not establish that our c-TTv2 and AGAD are equivalent to the published implementations, and the absence of a detected change does not show that AGAD is unaffected. In our implementation AGAD starts from a higher error at zero offset on this very coarse device.

The device presets against AIHWKIT itself (revision).

On a rented machine (never on our desk) we installed AIHWKIT from PyPI and drove its EcRamPresetDevice and EcRamMOPresetDevice through long up, down and alternating pulse schedules (500 devices each, with and without cycle-to-cycle noise), using its own plotting utilities. Our AIHWKIT-mode tile, driven through the same schedules, (largest mean difference for Li-ECRAM and for MO-ECRAM, in weight units; the pre-registered tolerance is \(\max(4\,\mathrm{SE},2\,\Delta w_{\min})\) at every stored pulse). The original field-copy mapping differs by up to for Li-ECRAM, mostly at the bounds (Appendix 7).

Main comparison on the repaired simulator

Tables 4 and 5 give the gap of every device–algorithm pairing over five seeds, against FP-SGD (the same network, learning rate, initialisation and data order with an exact update) and against digital Adam at its own selected learning rate. Every arm of a seed now shares its initial weights and its data order (checked by hash in every record). The FP-SGD learning rate is reused for every device arm: this is a restricted question (what happens when the FP-SGD rate is reused), not a fair-tuning comparison of the algorithms; Section 4.3 tunes each arm separately.

Against FP-SGD.

  • Plain SGD exceeded the line in of the cells of the four published devices, at the FP-selected learning rate.

  • All three tasks: pairings pass on every task: . No TTv2 pairing does: with the pulse reset, TTv2 fails on CIFAR on every published device.

  • Per task, , and of the device cells pass on MNIST, CIFAR and the LM. W/YSZ/WO\(_x\) fails on CIFAR and the LM with every algorithm, and MO-ECRAM fails on the LM.

  • Best cells: on MNIST ( pp), on CIFAR ( pp) and on the LM ( %). A negative gap whose interval includes zero is not evidence of superiority; and because these are the best of many cells, they are optimistic.

Against Adam.

Digital Adam is the stronger baseline. On the LM FP-SGD is  % worse in bits per byte than Adam, and no analog cell comes within the 5 % line of Adam: the best, , is  % worse ( of cells pass). On MNIST and CIFAR, where Adam and FP-SGD are close, and cells pass against Adam. No pairing passes all three tasks against Adam (). The analog results are therefore close to the FP-SGD comparator on these tasks, not to the best digital training in this study.

The margins.

The lines are practical non-inferiority margins, not equivalence: on MNIST a 2 pp loss from  % roughly doubles the error rate. UNRESOLVED means insufficient evidence against the margin, never adequate performance. The FP-SGD seed standard deviation is  pp on CIFAR and bits per byte on the LM.

What the update loses.

Two properties of the repaired simulator matter for reading these results.

  • Clipping. The TT family drives its \(A\) arrays at ten times the SGD rate, which exceeds the \(BL=31\) pulse budget in the largest layers: the mean lost fraction of the requested \(A\) update reaches  % in the CIFAR output layer and  % in the LM embedding (plain SGD at most  % in any layer’s mean). This is the hardware’s pulse budget, not a simulator error, but it means the effective \(A\) rate is capped in those layers.

  • Reset residual. With at most 62 pulses per weight, the pulse reset leaves a mean residual of nominal steps on the read \(A\) columns; reset pulses are  % of all pulses of the pulse-reset runs.

Ideal-device reference.

The same algorithms on an ideal device (symmetric, constant step, 1000 levels, no noise, no spread, exact reference) are the rows “Ideal 1000-level” of the tables (deviation R2). On MNIST every algorithm passes on it. On CIFAR and the LM none does: plain SGD loses  pp and  % (stochastic pulse updates on a 1000-level grid at the FP-SGD rate), and c-TTv2 and AGAD lose and  pp on CIFAR, far more than on the saturating Li-ECRAM and protonic-inspired devices. With the settings selected here, the TT family relies on the device’s own saturation as the decay of its accumulator; the ideal device has none. This is a property of these algorithm settings, not a general requirement that devices saturate: a sufficiently precise symmetric device can implement SGD, as the MNIST row shows.

Width

An earlier lane of this project saw the device gap grow with model width. Here every arm (protonic-inspired and Li-ECRAM, each with TTv2 and c-TTv2) gets its own learning rate at every width by the edge rule on validation, and then five test seeds per width; FP-SGD uses its own selected rate (Table 6). The initial weight scale grows with the width as in the rest of the paper (\(\alpha\) set from the initialisation bound), which is one mapping policy, not every fixed physical mapping.

The test.

The endpoint contrast \(D\) (the mean gap at the widest minus the narrowest width) is tested for equivalence within the gap lines (TOST at 5 %). The original paper’s “FLAT” label is withdrawn: it did not test equivalence and covered large non-monotonic changes.

CIFAR (\(c=16\), 32, 64).

arm is equivalent within \(\pm2\) pp (Li-ECRAM c-TTv2, \(D=\RVEFourCifarEcramLiTangTwoZeroOneEightCttvTwoD\) pp, 90 % interval [, ]); for arm there is no evidence of growth beyond the margin (protonic-inspired TTv2); arms are inconclusive (Li-ECRAM TTv2, \(D=\RVEFourCifarEcramLiTangTwoZeroOneEightTtvTwoD\) pp; protonic-inspired c-TTv2, \(D=\RVEFourCifarProtonicOnenTwoZeroTwoTwoCttvTwoD\) pp). Five seeds are not enough to settle a 2 pp margin on this subset.

The LM (\(d=64\), 128, 256).

All arms have a gap that shrinks with width (for example Li-ECRAM c-TTv2 from  % to  %). This is not a favourable scaling law: FP-SGD itself gets worse at the largest width under the fixed budget ( bits per byte at \(d=128\), at \(d=256\)), so a gap that turns negative partly measures a weaker baseline. Converged or quality-matched baselines would be needed to speak of scaling.

What can be said.

Across a factor of four in width, after per-arm learning-rate selection, our pre-registered test detected no growth of the device gap on either task; on CIFAR it established equivalence for one arm only, and on the LM the apparent shrinkage reflects the FP-SGD baseline at a fixed budget. Width is not resolved by this study.

Sensitivity against absolute lines

Around the protonic-inspired base we move one device property at a time (levels, step asymmetry, saturation \(\gamma\), write noise, reference error, retention) at the base sizes (CIFAR \(c=32\), LM \(d=128\)), three seeds paired with FP-SGD of the same seed, at FP-SGD’s learning rate. Every grid point is labelled against the absolute line (2 pp, 5 %), never against the base device’s own gap (Table 7). The asymmetry sweep is run twice: as before, where the symmetry point \(u^*=a/(2\gamma)\) moves toward the upper bound and the positive weight range shrinks (\(a=0.4\) at \(\gamma=0.2\) puts \(u^*\) on the bound); and with each device’s range re-centred on its symmetry point, so that only the up/down dynamics change.

The pre-registered sheet (TTv2) establishes no threshold.

Its base point is itself UNRESOLVED on both tasks ( pp on CIFAR,  % on the LM), so by the pre-registered rule every axis is “not established”. It still shows the confound the review pointed out: at \(a=0.4\) the gap is  pp on CIFAR when the symmetry point moves onto the bound, but  pp when it is held at mid-range. The earlier “asymmetry limit” was mostly lost weight range.

The chopped-TTv2 sheet (added after the main table, deviation R3).

On CIFAR the base passes ( pp, ), and the sheet establishes: step asymmetry up to with the symmetry point moving (at 0.4 the gap jumps to  pp, when \(u^*\) reaches the bound), and reference error up to of the half range. With the symmetry point held at mid-range only the base value is established (), but no point fails: up to \(a=0.4\) the mean gap stays at  pp and the intervals merely include the line. Levels, saturation, write noise and finite retention are not established: neighbouring grid values are UNRESOLVED with three seeds, while the clear failures are no saturation (\(\gamma=0\):  pp), strong saturation (\(\gamma=1\):  pp), reference error 0.2 ( pp) and retention of \(10^3\) updates or less. On the LM the base is with three seeds ( %; it passed with five seeds in the main table), so no LM threshold is established.

How to read the sheet.

These are one-at-a-time ranges around one base device, for one algorithm setting, at FP-SGD’s learning rate, with three seeds; they are exploratory, not fabrication tolerances. Combined deviations, other algorithm settings and independent device populations are not covered. A near-zero saturation fails here because, with these settings, the accumulator’s decay comes from the device (Section 4.2); it is not a general requirement for training.

Earlier development results

This study began as an exploratory screen with the same simulator (SGD and TTv2 only, 1–3 seeds). The screen is summarised here because some of its observations motivated the pre-registered experiments:

  • a CIFAR gap “just over 2 pp”;

  • a gap that “grows with width”;

  • a “pencil lead built today” that fails every task.

The earlier runs differ from this paper’s in three ways:

  • MNIST ran on a different GPU;

  • the LM’s selection split overlapped its training data (corrected here, Section 3.5);

  • CIFAR and the LM had one or two seeds.

With five seeds the earlier point estimates are mostly confirmed (Table 8), but the earlier pass/fail readings were not meaningful at that sample size. The CIFAR baseline’s seed-to-seed spread is comparable to the gap line itself.

The pessimistic memistor and the pencil-lead estimate were run only in the earlier screen. Both fail every task with SGD and with TTv2. Their specifications are estimates; the bench protocol of Appendix [app:bench] would replace the pencil-lead estimate by measurements.

The original results (superseded)

The first version of this paper reported the experiments below, run on the original simulator. An independent review found that this simulator (i) drew the initialisation, the data order and all device randomness from one shared random stream, so that two arms of the same seed did not share their initial weights or their data order; (ii) moved the TTv2 and c-TTv2 accumulator straight to its symmetry point while charging 62 pulses it did not apply; and (iii) copied the AIHWKIT preset fields into a model with different bounds and no slope spread. The results are kept here unchanged, as preliminary results of that simulator; the revised experiments of Sections 4.2–4.4 replace them. The diagnostic of Appendix 7 measures how much each repair moves them.

The original headline readings were: plain SGD failed on every published device and task; the Li-ECRAM fit and the protonic device passed or were unresolved on all three tasks with a Tiki-Taka-family algorithm; the original width classifier labelled every arm FLAT (which, as the review noted, is not evidence of equivalence); and the original specification sheet was mostly "not reachable", which led to a post hoc degradation sheet relative to an already imperfect base (a CIFAR base gap of  pp plus 2 pp admits gaps up to  pp). The best original analog LM cell was  % worse in bits per byte than digital Adam (a perplexity ratio of ).

Revision history and response to the independent review

History.

Version 1 (October 25, 2026) reported the experiments of Appendix 6. An independent technical review (October 26, 2026) recommended major revision with thirteen findings. Version 2 (this paper) answers them; the full response, finding by finding, with the checks that confirmed or qualified each one, is RESPONSE-TO-REVIEW.md in the release. The revision plan was committed before any revision run (PLAN-REVISION.md); its deviations R1–R are recorded in DEVIATIONS-PAPER.md.

What was repaired.

  1. Random streams. The initialisation, the data order, each tile’s device population and the pulse/noise draws now have separate generators; every record carries the hashes of its logical initialisation and data order, and every arm of a seed shares them (checked). The old single stream is kept as a mode that replays the original simulator bit for bit.

  2. The reset. The original reset moved \(A\) to its symmetry point and charged 62 pulses it never applied; applied through the device model those pulses leave  % of the displacement (from \(u=0.8\) the state only reaches , against a symmetry point of ; about alternating pulses would be needed for a hundredfold reduction). The repaired pulse reset applies and counts every pulse; the ideal reset is reported only as a labelled variant.

  3. The AIHWKIT presets are mapped one to one (shifted bounds, bound-scaled slopes, slope spread), and their pulse responses were compared with AIHWKIT’s own (Section 4.1): the mapping is .

  4. Measured, not assumed: the clipping of the pulse probabilities and the lost update are recorded per layer.

The checks of the repairs each fail on the old behaviour or a planted fault ( faults; on the desk and on every pod).

How much the repairs moved the original conclusions (diagnostic D1).

Table 15 runs the original and the repaired simulator side by side at the original selections, 3 seeds, on MNIST and a 10-epoch CIFAR slice ( runs).

  • The random streams moved individual cells by up to  pp on MNIST and  pp on CIFAR (material, i.e. more than 1 pp or a label change, in of and of cells). With three seeds this is within the noise: the repaired FP-SGD alone spans – % on the CIFAR slice. The matched controls did not reduce the paired-gap spread here (median against  pp).

  • The reset moved cells by up to  pp on MNIST and  pp on CIFAR. The ideal reset gave no hidden advantage: a physical reset (pulse, alternating pairs or none) had an equal or smaller gap in of cells.

  • The mapping moved Li-ECRAM by at most  pp on MNIST and  pp on CIFAR.

  • Unchanged: plain SGD fails by far (MNIST – pp, CIFAR slice – pp).

Wording withdrawn or narrowed.

“Near-digital” is not used. “Plain SGD fails on every device” became “every plain-SGD arm at the FP-selected learning rate exceeded the margin”. “The gap does not grow with width” became the equivalence statement of Section 4.3. “Two device properties decide” and “a few hundred levels suffice” became conditional statements about the sweeps of Section 4.4. “The memistor lacked density, speed and energy, not accuracy” became “an optimistic historical-device scenario attained useful accuracy in this simulator”. “32\(\times\) today with the periphery counted” became the conditional projection of Section [sec:energy]. “A bench replication” became “a proposed, unbuilt bench replication protocol”. “Every matrix is analog” became “the learned weight matrices use the device model; attention products and other operations are digital”.
